headline: Cantourage swings to profit as German prices fall; Australia squeezed
dek: Berlin's Cantourage posted €1.9M EBITDA on flat sales as German flower prices slide, while Australian growers say Canadian and Thai imports undercut them.
key_points: Cantourage's third-quarter revenue slipped to €19.9 million but EBITDA swung to €1.9 million from a €2.2 million loss as gross margin nearly doubled to 35.3%.
Germany fell to about 48% of Cantourage's sales; the UK and Poland now make up more than half, the company said.
In Australia, consultants and growers told StratCann that imports from Canada and Thailand are cheaper than local production, pushing some domestic producers to export or sell their sites.
Both markets point the same way: medical cannabis flower is becoming a price-driven commodity, and margins now come from supply contracts, brands and formats.
body: Two reports from opposite ends of the medical cannabis world this week told the same story about price. In Berlin, Cantourage Group said on 10 November that it earned an operating profit in the third quarter even as German flower prices kept falling, by selling less volume at higher margins and leaning on the UK. In Australia, growers and consultants told StratCann on 11 November that imported flower from Canada and Thailand now undercuts what many domestic cultivators can produce it for.

For producers trying to sell into regulated medical markets, the message is uncomfortable: the flower itself is turning into a commodity, and the winners are those with cheap supply, certified partners or their own brands.

Cantourage reported third-quarter revenue of €19.9 million, down from €20.3 million a year earlier. Gross margin rose to 35.3% from 18.1%, and EBITDA swung to €1.9 million from a loss of €2.2 million, a 9.5% margin. For the first nine months, revenue was €62.3 million and EBITDA €6.8 million. The company ended September with net cash of €10.8 million.

Germany produced €9.5 million of quarterly revenue, about 48% of the total. Cantourage blamed falling flower prices and more competitors, and said it is choosing premium ranges over volume at any cost. The UK contributed €9.3 million and Poland €1.1 million. Brokerage NuWays noted that both were down from the second quarter: UK sales slipped as the market switched to a rule allowing only EU-GMP certified products, and Polish sales halved as average prices fell about 25%.

NuWays also reported that management now points to the lower end of its 2026 guidance of €85 million to €95 million in sales and €10 million to €12 million in adjusted EBITDA. By MetaFlora's calculation, reaching the bottom of the sales range needs about €22.7 million in the fourth quarter, roughly 14% more than the third. German pharmacy title Apotheke Adhoc noted the company coped better than rivals with Germany's removal of flower from statutory health insurance reimbursement, thanks to its focus on self-paying and telemedicine patients.
> Medical flower is following the path of every other crop: the margin moves to whoever controls certified supply and the brand.

The price pressure is market-wide. Business of Cannabis reported on 3 November that the average unweighted price of medical flower in Germany fell from €7.70 a gram in September 2025 to €6.00 in September 2026, about 22%, while the number of flower products on the market rose about 73%, as we reported on 8 November. Cantourage's response has been to sign supply deals: it completed EU-GMP certification projects with All Nations, Green Karat and LOT420, each with five-year exclusive supply terms, and launched an own brand plus extracts and a distillate that pharmacies can compound into other forms.
## Australia: built for a market that moved

In Australia the pressure comes from imports. Liz Warburton of Nativa Consulting told StratCann that competing with imports on price is the single largest issue for Australian cultivators, and that many growers' production costs exceed the prices brands can get from Canadian or Thai suppliers.

Consultants pointed to structural costs. Cate Hall, who chairs the Australian Cannabis Cultivator Guild, said cultivators pay between A$29,000 and A$60,000 a year to keep their licences regardless of size, while importers carry no comparable cultivation costs. Growers described waiting a year for a licence and another year for a permit, and nine months or more for approval of minor site changes. Canada's advantage is a mature industry with efficient facilities; Thailand's is cheaper labour, climate and lighter regulation; both pay less for electricity, according to the experts StratCann interviewed.

Australian producers are responding by chasing exports, where prices are also falling, launching their own brands or, in some cases, selling their facilities at a loss, Warburton said. Chris Liddy of Solum Advisory cautioned that not every large early investment was a mistake, and that efficient producers can still justify theirs.

Put side by side, the two reports show where the medical cannabis value chain is heading. Large, efficient Canadian growers and low-cost Thai supply are setting a floor price in import markets from Germany to Australia. Distributors such as Cantourage protect margins through exclusive certified supply and their own brands, while high-cost domestic growers in markets like Australia struggle to compete on price.

Cantourage still owes its audited 2025 group accounts under its new IFRS reporting and has not named a successor to chief executive Philip Schetter, NuWays noted. Its fourth quarter will show whether the UK's EU-GMP rule helps certified suppliers as expected. In Germany, Berlin's proposed limits on medical cannabis telemedicine and mail-order remain stalled in the coalition. In Australia, watch for further facility sales and whether regulators respond to calls for clearer cultivation rules.
